newsitem.title: USA: Tungsten market faces key choices - Avocet.
newsitem.headline: Tungsten market faces key choices - Avocet.

text.p: Calling on official stockpiles to plug the looming gap in tungsten supply will just shore up problems for the future, said Robert Bunting, president of Avocet Tungsten Inc.

"Existing mines are running out of ore, and if you hold the price down by selling stockpiles, the piper will pay in five to ten years time when all the mines are out of ore and the stockpiles run out," Bunting told Reuters.
Avocet Tungsten is part of Avocet Mining Plc, the largest western tungsten producer with mines and operations in Peru, the U.S. and Portugal.
Tungsten producers met in Nanchang, China, Nov 1-3 where they vowed to continue lobbying government stockpiles in China, the U.S. and Russia to tread carefully in the market.
"We are talking more of restraint rather than cessation of sales, to be realistic," Bunting said.
The producers, who also want to set up a permanent international tungsten mining association to gather output data, were quick to reject accusations of creating a cartel.
"We have no agreement or understanding or anything like that, or that we would mutually work together to push the price up," said Bunting.
No metal has been sold from any of the three official stockpiles since mid-1995.
Tungsten is mostly used to make cutting equipment, light bulb filaments, heavy metal components, catalysts and tool steels. World production is dominated by China.

Bunting said global primary tungsten production will be 27,000 tonnes this year, with primary metal consumption of about 38,800 tonnes. The 11,000-tonne gap will be filled by what is left of surplus free market stocks.

"The market should be balanced by the end of this year," Bunting said. Chinese and Russian mines have relatively few stock left. "The cross over point is the end of this year when we will not have stocks to fill the void. Beyond that we eat into pipeline inventory."
Bunting forecast a supply gap of 14,000 tonnes of primary metal next year if current production and offtake continue.

All Russian mines are shut except Lermontov in which Avocet has a 10.6 percent stake. The mine started up at the end of October and will produce 120 tonnes of contained tungsten a month "until they run out of money," Bunting said.

The Russian stockpile was estimated by some as down to 5,000 tonnes of contained metal. "I would be surprised if it was that low," Bunting said. "But some of the Russian stockpile is radioactive and possibly not going to be touched by anybody."
Bunting believed Chinese official tungsten stockpiles are low. The stockpile began replenishing itself after buying 3,000 tonnes of tungsten ore from domestic mines.
The U.S. stockpile totals 37,500 tonnes of contained tungsten but there is no authority to sell tungsten in fiscal 1997.
If producers persuade official stockpiles not to sell, it seems inevitable tungsten prices will rise to pay for new production.

"The very best mines in the world can barely produce at today's price on a cash basis let alone full costs," Bunting said. Intermediate product, ammonium paratungstate (APT) prices have tumbled to $50 to $54 per tonne.
To cover exploration, building plant, marketing and production costs, the price of APT would have to be about $130 per mtu for a "reasonable return," Bunting said.
